claim: AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs in adult stellate cells (P35-57) have significantly smaller amplitude (24 ± 2 pA) compared to immature stellate cells (P13-19) (48 ± 7 pA).
source: In immature SCs, the average mEPSC amplitude was 48 ± 7 pA, with 10–90% rise and decay times (τdecay, see Methods) of 0.16 ± 0.01 and 0.68 ± 0.06 ms, respectively. In contrast, mEPSCs from adult SCs were smaller 24 ± 2 pA (p < 0.05), with slower rising (0.24 ± 0.02 ms; p < 0.05) and decaying kinetics (τdecay = 1.31 ± 0.14 ms; p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of mEPSC amplitudes in immature and adult stellate cells, with statistical significance indicated.

claim: AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs in adult stellate cells have slower 10-90% rise time (0.24 ± 0.02 ms) compared to immature stellate cells (0.16 ± 0.01 ms).
source: In immature SCs, the average mEPSC amplitude was 48 ± 7 pA, with 10–90% rise and decay times (τdecay, see Methods) of 0.16 ± 0.01 and 0.68 ± 0.06 ms, respectively. In contrast, mEPSCs from adult SCs were smaller 24 ± 2 pA (p < 0.05), with slower rising (0.24 ± 0.02 ms; p < 0.05) and decaying kinetics (τdecay = 1.31 ± 0.14 ms; p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of mEPSC rise times in immature and adult stellate cells, with statistical significance indicated.

claim: AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs in adult stellate cells have slower decay kinetics (τdecay = 1.31 ± 0.14 ms) compared to immature stellate cells (τdecay = 0.68 ± 0.06 ms).
source: In immature SCs, the average mEPSC amplitude was 48 ± 7 pA, with 10–90% rise and decay times (τdecay, see Methods) of 0.16 ± 0.01 and 0.68 ± 0.06 ms, respectively. In contrast, mEPSCs from adult SCs were smaller 24 ± 2 pA (p < 0.05), with slower rising (0.24 ± 0.02 ms; p < 0.05) and decaying kinetics (τdecay = 1.31 ± 0.14 ms; p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of mEPSC decay kinetics in immature and adult stellate cells, with statistical significance indicated.

claim: mEPSC frequency is similar between immature and adult stellate cells (1.37 ± 0.27 Hz vs. 1.14 ± 0.13 Hz).
source: We found that AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs occurred with a similar frequency at both ages (1.37 ± 0.27 vs. 1.14 ± 0.13 Hz, p > 0.05), but mEPSCs were significantly smaller and slower in the adult (Figure 1A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of mEPSC frequency in immature and adult stellate cells, with no statistical significance indicated.

claim: Application of γDGG (1 mM) reduced mEPSC peak amplitude similarly in immature (44.42% ± 4.36%) and adult (42.38% ± 3.69%) stellate cells.
source: Application of a submaximal concentration of γDGG (1 mM) reduced mEPSC peak amplitude (Figure 1D, paired p < 0.05) similarly at both ages (44.42% ± 4.36%, n = 7 in the immature vs. 42.38% ± 3.69%, n = 9 in the adult, p > 0.05; Figure 1E), with no apparent effect on mEPSC kinetics (Figure 1F, paired p > 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of mEPSC amplitude reduction following γDGG application in immature and adult stellate cells.

claim: γDGG application had no apparent effect on mEPSC kinetics in either immature or adult stellate cells.
source: Application of a submaximal concentration of γDGG (1 mM) reduced mEPSC peak amplitude (Figure 1D, paired p < 0.05) similarly at both ages (44.42% ± 4.36%, n = 7 in the immature vs. 42.38% ± 3.69%, n = 9 in the adult, p > 0.05; Figure 1E), with no apparent effect on mEPSC kinetics (Figure 1F, paired p > 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements showing no significant change in mEPSC kinetics following γDGG application.

claim: The decreased amplitude and slowing of mEPSCs during development is unlikely due to a change in the synaptic glutamate concentration.
source: This result suggests that the decreased amplitude and slowing of mEPSCs is unlikely due to a change in the synaptic [Glut].
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the γDGG experiment results showing similar effects at both ages.

claim: Immature stellate cell dendrite diameters range from 0.26 to 0.93 µm with a mean of 0.47 ± 0.01 µm.
source: Diameters ranged from 0.26 to 0.93 µm with a mean of 0.47 ± 0.01 µm (n = 93 dendritic segments of 18 neurons; Figure 2B), which is close to the average adult value of 0.41 ± 0.02 µm (range 0.24–0.9 μm, n = 78 dendrites; data from Abrahamsson et al., 2012; p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of dendritic diameters from confocal images of immature stellate cells.

claim: Adult stellate cell dendrite diameters have an average value of 0.41 ± 0.02 µm (range 0.24–0.9 μm).
source: Diameters ranged from 0.26 to 0.93 µm with a mean of 0.47 ± 0.01 µm (n = 93 dendritic segments of 18 neurons; Figure 2B), which is close to the average adult value of 0.41 ± 0.02 µm (range 0.24–0.9 μm, n = 78 dendrites; data from Abrahamsson et al., 2012; p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous measurements from Abrahamsson et al., 2012.

claim: The membrane time constant of immature stellate cells is 19 ± 2.2 ms.
source: Using the estimated 0.47 μm dendritic diameter, a membrane resistance (Rm) of 20,000 Ω.cm2 matching that measured immature SCs membrane time constant τm of 19 ± 2.2 ms, n = 16, which was similar to a τm of 17 ± 2.7 ms for adult SCs (Abrahamsson et al., 2012) and an internal resistivity Ri ranging from 100 to 200 Ω.cm, we calculated the steady-state dendritic space constant (λ) to be between 343 and 485 µm, which is 3- to 5-fold longer than the actual dendritic length.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of membrane time constant in immature stellate cells.

claim: The membrane time constant of adult stellate cells is 17 ± 2.7 ms.
source: Using the estimated 0.47 μm dendritic diameter, a membrane resistance (Rm) of 20,000 Ω.cm2 matching that measured immature SCs membrane time constant τm of 19 ± 2.2 ms, n = 16, which was similar to a τm of 17 ± 2.7 ms for adult SCs (Abrahamsson et al., 2012) and an internal resistivity Ri ranging from 100 to 200 Ω.cm, we calculated the steady-state dendritic space constant (λ) to be between 343 and 485 µm, which is 3- to 5-fold longer than the actual dendritic length.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous measurements from Abrahamsson et al., 2012.

claim: The steady-state dendritic space constant of immature stellate cells is between 343 and 485 µm, which is 3- to 5-fold longer than the actual dendritic length.
source: Using the estimated 0.47 μm dendritic diameter, a membrane resistance (Rm) of 20,000 Ω.cm2 matching that measured immature SCs membrane time constant τm of 19 ± 2.2 ms, n = 16, which was similar to a τm of 17 ± 2.7 ms for adult SCs (Abrahamsson et al., 2012) and an internal resistivity Ri ranging from 100 to 200 Ω.cm, we calculated the steady-state dendritic space constant (λ) to be between 343 and 485 µm, which is 3- to 5-fold longer than the actual dendritic length.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using measured dendritic diameter, membrane resistance, and internal resistivity.

claim: The frequency-dependent space constant (λf) of immature stellate cells is between 46 and 60 µm for Ri of 100–200 Ω.cm.
source: However, the frequency-dependent space constant (λf; assuming that rapid mEPSCs are well approximated by a 1 kHz sine wave) was calculated to be between 46 and 60 µm (for Ri of 100–200 Ω.cm, respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using measured parameters and assumptions about mEPSC frequency content.

claim: The frequency-dependent space constant values are similar to the dendritic lengths of immature stellate cells and suggest that somatic recording of EPSC originating in dendrites may be smaller and slower due to electrotonic cable filtering.
source: These values are similar to the dendritic lengths of immature SCs (Figure 6) and suggest that, like in adult SCs (Abrahamsson et al., 2012), somatic recording of EPSC originating in dendrites may be smaller and slower due to electrotonic cable filtering.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of calculated space constants with measured dendritic lengths and inference about cable filtering effects.

claim: Simulated qEPSCs evoked from synapses located on dendrites at 45 µm from the soma were 48% smaller than those at the soma.
source: Simulated qEPSCs were large and fast for synapses located at the soma (magenta trace, Figure 2C), but qEPSCs evoked from synapses located on the dendrites (gray trace; at 45 µm from the soma, Ri of 150 Ω.cm) were 48 % smaller and showed a 195 % slower rise time and a 180 % slower half-width.
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations using an idealized stellate cell model.

claim: Simulated qEPSCs evoked from synapses located on dendrites at 45 µm from the soma showed a 195% slower rise time compared to somatic synapses.
source: Simulated qEPSCs were large and fast for synapses located at the soma (magenta trace, Figure 2C), but qEPSCs evoked from synapses located on the dendrites (gray trace; at 45 µm from the soma, Ri of 150 Ω.cm) were 48 % smaller and showed a 195 % slower rise time and a 180 % slower half-width.
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations using an idealized stellate cell model.

claim: Simulated qEPSCs evoked from synapses located on dendrites at 45 µm from the soma showed a 180% slower half-width compared to somatic synapses.
source: Simulated qEPSCs were large and fast for synapses located at the soma (magenta trace, Figure 2C), but qEPSCs evoked from synapses located on the dendrites (gray trace; at 45 µm from the soma, Ri of 150 Ω.cm) were 48 % smaller and showed a 195 % slower rise time and a 180 % slower half-width.
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations using an idealized stellate cell model.

claim: Dendritic filtering is associated with a large increase in the local synaptic depolarization that would substantially reduce the local driving force during synaptic transmission onto dendrites.
source: This dendritic filtering was also associated with a large increase in the local synaptic depolarization (green trace, Figure 2C) that would substantially reduce the local driving force during synaptic transmission onto dendrites, potentially causing a sublinear read-out of the underlying conductance, as observed in adult SCs (Abrahamsson et al., 2012; Tran-Van-Minh et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations and cited previous observations in adult stellate cells.

claim: Beyond ~40 µm from the soma, there is little additional cable filtering of synaptic responses.
source: Examination of the amplitude, rise time, and half-width as a function of synapse distance shows that beyond ~40 µm there is little additional cable filtering (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of simulation results showing distance-dependent filtering properties.

claim: Stimulation of somatic synapses in immature stellate cells produced qEPSCs with a mean peak amplitude of 62 ± 3 pA, a 10–90% rise time of 0.14 ± 0.004 ms, and a half-width of 0.60 ± 0.02 ms.
source: When stimulating somatic synapses, qEPSCs recorded at the soma had a mean peak amplitude of 62 ± 3 pA, a 10–90% rise time of 0.14 ± 0.004 ms, and a half-width of 0.60 ± 0.02 ms (n = 25; Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of qEPSCs evoked by somatic synapse stimulation in immature stellate cells.

claim: Stimulation of distal synapses in the outer third of the dendritic field of immature stellate cells produced qEPSCs with a mean amplitude of 46 ± 3 pA, a 10–90% rise time of 0.24 ± 0.012 ms, and a half-width of 0.88 ± 0.04 ms.
source: In contrast, the stimulation of distal synapses, in the outer third of the dendritic field, produced somatically recorded qEPSCs that were significantly smaller (mean amplitude: 46 ± 3 pA) and slower (10–90% rise time of 0.24 ± 0.012 ms and a half-width of 0.88 ± 0.04 ms; n = 18; all p < 0.05, Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of qEPSCs evoked by distal dendritic synapse stimulation in immature stellate cells.

claim: The difference in qEPSC amplitude and time-course between somatic and dendritic synapses in immature stellate cells is consistent with cable filtering.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with cable filtering of EPSCs as they propagate along dendrites in immature SCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental measurements showing distance-dependent changes in qEPSC properties.

claim: PSD area is constant along the somatodendritic axis of immature stellate cells.
source: PSD area was constant along somatodendritic axes (Figure 3G), ruling out synaptic scaling as a mechanism for reducing dendrite-evoked qEPSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy measurements of PSD area at different distances from the soma.

claim: The difference in qEPSC amplitude and time-course observed between somatic and dendritic synapses in immature stellate cells is likely due to cable filtering.
source: Thus, the difference in qEPSC amplitude and time-course observed between somatic and dendritic synapses in immature SCs is likely due to cable filtering.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing constant PSD area and distance-dependent qEPSC properties.

claim: Somatic qEPSCs in immature stellate cells are 41% larger than those in adult stellate cells (62.3 ± 3.3 pA vs. 44 ± 2.4 pA).
source: In immature SCs, somatic qEPSCs were 41 % larger than those in adult SCs (62.3 ± 3.3 pA, n = 25 vs. 44 ± 2.4 pA, n = 12, Abrahamsson et al., 2012), p < 0.05, Figure 4A and B, but with no difference in the half-width (0.60 ± 0.02 ms, n = 25 vs. 0.59 ± 0.06 ms, n = 12, p > 0.05, Figure 4B) suggesting a reduction in postsynaptic strength but no change in kinetics.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of somatic qEPSCs in immature stellate cells and cited measurements from adult stellate cells.

claim: There is no difference in somatic qEPSC half-width between immature and adult stellate cells (0.60 ± 0.02 ms vs. 0.59 ± 0.06 ms).
source: In immature SCs, somatic qEPSCs were 41 % larger than those in adult SCs (62.3 ± 3.3 pA, n = 25 vs. 44 ± 2.4 pA, n = 12, Abrahamsson et al., 2012), p < 0.05, Figure 4A and B, but with no difference in the half-width (0.60 ± 0.02 ms, n = 25 vs. 0.59 ± 0.06 ms, n = 12, p > 0.05, Figure 4B) suggesting a reduction in postsynaptic strength but no change in kinetics.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of somatic qEPSC half-width in immature stellate cells and cited measurements from adult stellate cells.

claim: The developmental reduction in somatic qEPSC amplitude suggests a reduction in postsynaptic strength but no change in kinetics.
source: In immature SCs, somatic qEPSCs were 41 % larger than those in adult SCs (62.3 ± 3.3 pA, n = 25 vs. 44 ± 2.4 pA, n = 12, Abrahamsson et al., 2012), p < 0.05, Figure 4A and B, but with no difference in the half-width (0.60 ± 0.02 ms, n = 25 vs. 0.59 ± 0.06 ms, n = 12, p > 0.05, Figure 4B) suggesting a reduction in postsynaptic strength but no change in kinetics.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental measurements showing amplitude reduction without kinetic changes.

claim: Mean somatic PSD size in immature stellate cells is 0.039 ± 0.002 μm2, which is 39% larger than that of adult stellate cells (0.028 ± 0.0015 μm2).
source: In immature SCs, mean somatic PSD size was 0.039 ± 0.002 μm2 (n = 83 synapses; Figure 4C), which is 39 % larger than that of adult SCs (0.028 ± 0.0015 μm2, n = 97, p < 0.05; data obtained by the same method from Abrahamsson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy measurements of PSD area in immature stellate cells and cited measurements from adult stellate cells.

claim: The developmental reduction in PSD size is similar to the amplitude reduction of recorded somatic qEPSC and will contribute to the developmental reduction in mEPSC.
source: The developmental reduction in PSD size is similar to the amplitude reduction of recorded somatic qEPSC and thus will contribute to the developmental reduction in mEPSC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity between PSD size reduction and qEPSC amplitude reduction.

claim: The 10-90% rise time of somatic qEPSCs is slower in immature stellate cells compared to adult (0.14 ± 0.02 ms vs. 0.12 ± 0.004 ms), consistent with larger immature synapses.
source: This is supported experimentally by a slower 10–90% rise time in immature SCs compared to adult (0.14 ± 0.02 ms, n = 25 vs. 0.12 ± 0.004, n = 12, p < 0.05; Figure 4B, middle panel), consistent with larger immature synapses (Cathala et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of qEPSC rise time and cited previous observations about synapse size effects.

claim: Fewer synaptic AMPARs cannot explain the observed change in mEPSC time-course during development.
source: However, fewer synaptic AMPARs cannot explain the observed change in mEPSC time-course.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that AMPAR number reduction would not account for kinetic changes.

claim: In immature stellate cells, the mean mEPSC decay (τdecay = 0.68 ± 0.06 ms) is similar to the qEPSC decay from somatic synapses (half-width = 0.60 ± 0.02 ms).
source: Specifically, in immature SCs the mean mEPSC decay (τdecay = 0.68 ± 0.06 ms) is similar to the qEPSC decay from somatic synapses (half-width = 0.60 ± 0.02 ms; p > 0.05), but significantly different from those of dendritic synapses (half-width = 0.88 ± 0.04 ms; p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental measurements of mEPSC and qEPSC kinetics.

claim: In immature stellate cells, the mean mEPSC decay is significantly different from that of dendritic synapses (τdecay = 0.68 ± 0.06 ms vs. half-width = 0.88 ± 0.04 ms).
source: Specifically, in immature SCs the mean mEPSC decay (τdecay = 0.68 ± 0.06 ms) is similar to the qEPSC decay from somatic synapses (half-width = 0.60 ± 0.02 ms; p > 0.05), but significantly different from those of dendritic synapses (half-width = 0.88 ± 0.04 ms; p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental measurements of mEPSC and qEPSC kinetics.

claim: Synaptic responses from distal synapses do not participate significantly to the mean mEPSC in immature stellate cells.
source: This suggests that synaptic responses from distal synapses do not participate significantly to the mean mEPSC at this developmental stage.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity between mEPSC and somatic qEPSC kinetics.

claim: In adult stellate cells, the mEPSC decay (τdecay = 1.31 ± 0.14 ms) is close to the dendritic qEPSC decay (half-width = 1.14 ± 1.92).
source: In contrast, the adult mEPSC decay (τdecay = 1.31 ± 0.14 ms) is close to the dendritic qEPSC decay (half-width = 1.14 ± 1.92, p > 0.05), but significantly different from that of somatic synapses (half-width = 0.59 ± 0.06, p < 0.05), estimated previously (Abrahamsson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental measurements of mEPSC and qEPSC kinetics, with citation of previous measurements.

claim: In adult stellate cells, the mEPSC decay is significantly different from that of somatic synapses (τdecay = 1.31 ± 0.14 ms vs. half-width = 0.59 ± 0.06 ms).
source: In contrast, the adult mEPSC decay (τdecay = 1.31 ± 0.14 ms) is close to the dendritic qEPSC decay (half-width = 1.14 ± 1.92, p > 0.05), but significantly different from that of somatic synapses (half-width = 0.59 ± 0.06, p < 0.05), estimated previously (Abrahamsson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental measurements of mEPSC and qEPSC kinetics, with citation of previous measurements.

claim: mEPSCs in adult stellate cells arise more often from more distal synapses.
source: These results are consistent with mEPSCs in adult SCs arising more often from more distal synapses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity between adult mEPSC and dendritic qEPSC kinetics.

claim: Adult stellate cells have ~80% more Venus-tagged PSD95 puncta than immature stellate cells (582 ± 48 vs. 324 ± 21).
source: Venus-tagged PSD95 puncta within the soma and dendritic tree of nine immature and eight adult 3D-reconstructed SCs (Figure 5G), showed ~80 % more puncta on adult SCs (582 ± 48 puncta vs. 324 ± 21 in immature SCs, p < 0.05; of which 27 ± 3.2 and 21.17 ± 2.5 are at the soma of immature and adult SCs, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Venus-tagged PSD95 puncta from 2P imaging of immature and adult stellate cells.

claim: In immature stellate cells, ~80% of synapses are within 35 µm of the soma, in contrast to only ~40% in adult stellate cells.
source: In immature SCs, ~ 80 % are within 35 µm of the soma, in contrast to only ~40 % this close to the soma in adult SCs (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of synapse distribution from Venus-tagged PSD95 puncta mapping.

claim: Puncta density remained constant across the dendritic tree at both immature and adult ages.
source: However, the ratio of detected puncta (Figure 6B) to dendritic segments (Figure 6C) shows that puncta density remained constant across the dendritic tree at both ages (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of the ratio of puncta to dendritic segments at different distances from the soma.

claim: Increased dendritic complexity during stellate cell maturation is responsible for a prominent shift toward distal synapses in adult stellate cells.
source: These data demonstrate that increased dendritic complexity during SC maturation is responsible for a prominent shift toward distal synapses in adult SCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that synapse density is constant but dendritic branching increases.

claim: If mEPSCs were generated from a homogeneous probability of release across all synapses, the bias toward distal synapses in adult stellate cells will generate quantal responses that experience stronger cable filtering.
source: Therefore, if mEPSCs were generated from a homogeneous probability of release across all synapses, the bias toward distal synapses in adult SC will generate quantal responses that experience stronger cable filtering.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed distal bias in synapse distribution and known cable filtering properties.

claim: Simulated mean mEPSCs were smaller in adult stellate cells than in immature stellate cells (26.0 ± 0.6 pA vs. 52.2 ± 0.4 pA for Ri 150 Ω.cm).
source: As a result, the mean mEPSC was smaller in adult SCs than in immature SCs (26.0 ± 0.6 pA, n = 9 dendrites vs. 52.2 ± 0.4 pA, n = 7 for Ri 150 Ω.cm) and its time-course had slower rise (10–90% rise time = 0.24 ± 0.05 vs. 0.17 ± 0.01 ms) and decay (half-width = 1.11 ± 0.04 vs. 0.77 ± 0.01 ms; for all p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations incorporating experimentally determined synapse distributions.

claim: Simulated mean mEPSCs had slower rise time in adult stellate cells than in immature stellate cells (10–90% rise time = 0.24 ± 0.05 ms vs. 0.17 ± 0.01 ms).
source: As a result, the mean mEPSC was smaller in adult SCs than in immature SCs (26.0 ± 0.6 pA, n = 9 dendrites vs. 52.2 ± 0.4 pA, n = 7 for Ri 150 Ω.cm) and its time-course had slower rise (10–90% rise time = 0.24 ± 0.05 vs. 0.17 ± 0.01 ms) and decay (half-width = 1.11 ± 0.04 vs. 0.77 ± 0.01 ms; for all p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations incorporating experimentally determined synapse distributions.

claim: Simulated mean mEPSCs had slower decay in adult stellate cells than in immature stellate cells (half-width = 1.11 ± 0.04 ms vs. 0.77 ± 0.01 ms).
source: As a result, the mean mEPSC was smaller in adult SCs than in immature SCs (26.0 ± 0.6 pA, n = 9 dendrites vs. 52.2 ± 0.4 pA, n = 7 for Ri 150 Ω.cm) and its time-course had slower rise (10–90% rise time = 0.24 ± 0.05 vs. 0.17 ± 0.01 ms) and decay (half-width = 1.11 ± 0.04 vs. 0.77 ± 0.01 ms; for all p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations incorporating experimentally determined synapse distributions.

claim: Distally generated qEPSCs dominate the mean mEPSC more strongly in adult than in immature stellate cells, making the mean mEPSC smaller and slower in adult stellate cells.
source: Thus, distally generated qEPSCds dominate the mean mEPSC more strongly in adult than in immature SCs, making the mean mEPSC smaller and slower in adult SCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results showing the contribution of distal synapses to mean mEPSC.

claim: The simulated mean mEPSCs lay within one standard deviation of measured experimental mEPSC values.
source: Moreover, the simulated mean mEPSCs lay within one standard deviation of measured experimental mEPSC values (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental measurements.

claim: By implementing the experimentally observed synapse distributions in simulations, the experimental mean mEPSCs could be reproduced.
source: Thus, by implementing the experimentally observed synapse distributions in our simulations, we could reproduce the experimental mean mEPSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the agreement between simulated and experimental mEPSCs when using measured synapse distributions.

claim: Developmental increases in dendritic branching complexity, provided that synapse density is homogeneous, can account for the changes in mEPSC kinetics.
source: These results demonstrate that developmental increases in dendritic branching complexity, provided that synapse density is homogeneous, can account for the changes in mEPSC kinetics (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results showing that synapse distribution changes can explain mEPSC kinetic changes.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR) for somatic synapses in immature stellate cells is 2.1 ± 0.1.
source: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR; the ratio of the amplitudes of the second vs. the first EPSC) was 2.1 ± 0.1 for somatic synapses (n = 10) and decreased to 1.8 ± 0.1 for distal dendritic synapses (n = 15; p < 0.05; Figure 8A), consistent with sublinear integration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of paired-pulse facilitation at somatic synapses.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR) for distal dendritic synapses in immature stellate cells is 1.8 ± 0.1.
source: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR; the ratio of the amplitudes of the second vs. the first EPSC) was 2.1 ± 0.1 for somatic synapses (n = 10) and decreased to 1.8 ± 0.1 for distal dendritic synapses (n = 15; p < 0.05; Figure 8A), consistent with sublinear integration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of paired-pulse facilitation at distal dendritic synapses.

claim: The decrease in PPR from somatic to distal dendritic synapses in immature stellate cells is consistent with sublinear integration.
source: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR; the ratio of the amplitudes of the second vs. the first EPSC) was 2.1 ± 0.1 for somatic synapses (n = 10) and decreased to 1.8 ± 0.1 for distal dendritic synapses (n = 15; p < 0.05; Figure 8A), consistent with sublinear integration.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed PPR gradient and its known relationship to dendritic integration.

claim: Immature stellate cell dendrites display an STP gradient, suggesting that they are capable of sublinear integration.
source: These findings show that immature SC dendrites also display an STP gradient, suggesting that they are capable of sublinear integration.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed PPR gradient between soma and dendrites.

claim: Simulated subthreshold I/O plots showed that sim eEPSPs in the soma and dendrites were less than the linear sum of eEPSPs.
source: I/O plots showed that sim eEPSPs in the soma and dendrites were less than the linear sum of eEPSPs (dashed line).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations of subthreshold synaptic integration.

claim: Sublinear summation was apparent for dendritic eEPSPs generated from synaptic conductances equivalent to one quantum for dendritic synapses and became more pronounced for distal synapses.
source: This sublinear summation was apparent for dendritic eEPSPs generated from synaptic conductances equivalent to one quantum for dendritic synapses and became more pronounced for distal synapses (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations showing distance-dependent sublinearity.

claim: The sublinearity increased with increasing number of simultaneously activated quanta.
source: The sublinearity increased with increasing number of simultaneously activated quanta.
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations showing input-dependent sublinearity.

claim: Simulations show that immature dendrites demonstrate sublinear summation, supporting experimental difference between somatic and dendritic STP.
source: These simulations show that immature dendrites demonstrate sublinear summation, supporting experimental difference between somatic and dendritic STP (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results that are consistent with experimental observations.

claim: Dendritic sublinearity was larger in adult stellate cells than in immature stellate cells for all postsynaptic strengths.
source: While both immature and adult SCs exhibited sublinear integration, dendritic sublinearity was larger in adult SCs for all postsynaptic strengths, supporting an increased difference between the two layers of integration (i.e., soma vs. dendrite).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations comparing sublinearity at the two developmental stages.

claim: The smaller difference in sublinearity between soma and dendrite in the immature stellate cell resulted from both fewer distal synapses and the larger gsyn.
source: The smaller difference in sublinearity between soma and dendrite in the immature SC resulted from both fewer distal synapses and the larger gsyn.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results showing the combined effects of synapse distribution and conductance.

claim: The developmental increase in dendritic field complexity and decreased postsynaptic strength together contribute to the establishment of a two-stage integration model.
source: Thus, the developmental increase in dendritic field complexity and decreased postsynaptic strength together contribute to the establishment of a two-stage integration model and provide a cellular substrate for a developmental increase in computational power of SCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined effects of morphological and functional changes observed during development.

claim: Developmental changes in synapse distribution within dendritic trees can generate isolated electrical compartments that enable nonlinear integration of local synaptic responses.
source: In particular, the cable properties of dendritic trees can generate isolated electrical compartments that enable nonlinear integration of local synaptic responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discussion of cable properties and their role in compartmentalization, combined with the observed developmental changes in synapse distribution.

claim: Cerebellar stellate cells are parvalbumin-positive (PV+) GABAergic interneurons.
source: Cerebellar stellate cells (SCs) are parvalbumin-positive (PV+) GABAergic interneurons that share anatomical and functional features with PV+ interneurons found in the neocortex and hippocampus (Hu et al., 2014) such as high fidelity of synaptic transmission (Chen and Regehr, 2000), expression of Ca2+-permeable α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA receptors) (AMPARs) (Soler-Llavina and Sabatini, 2006), low levels of synaptic N-méthyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) ( Clark and Cull-Candy, 2002), and weakly excitable dendrites (Abrahamsson et al., 2012), which together provide precise temporal control of principal neuron activity (Mittmann et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001).
